blocks.text:
Design the real-time collaborative document editor behind something like Google Docs, where several people can open the same document and type at the same time, each seeing everyone else's changes appear live, and all of them ending up with the exact same final text no matter what order their keystrokes actually happened to arrive in. This is a genuinely different kind of problem from the messaging systems covered elsewhere in this category. WhatsApp and Slack move a message from one person to a group, and that message never has to be reconciled against another message, it just gets delivered. Google Docs has to reconcile two people's edits to the very same sentence, sometimes to the very same character, and still land on one document that both of them agree is correct.

The centerpiece of this design is an algorithm called Operational Transformation, which is the actual technique the real Google Docs was built on. Everything else in this document, the architecture, the sharding, the consistency model, exists to support that one algorithm running correctly and fast.

blocks.text: Multiple users need to be able to edit the same document concurrently and see each other's edits appear in real time. Every user's cursor and selection position should be visible to everyone else currently in the document. A user who was editing offline should be able to reconnect and have their local changes merged cleanly into whatever happened while they were away. The system should keep a version history a user can browse and restore from. Access to a document should be controllable at three levels: view only, comment, and full edit.

blocks.text: The five qualities that matter most here look almost like the mirror image of a chat system's priorities.
blocks.content: The five qualities that matter most here look almost like the mirror image of a chat system's priorities.

blocks.alt: Strong convergent consistency, low local-echo latency, per-document availability, durability, and offline tolerance

blocks.text: Consistency is the one that flips hardest compared to a chat app: every single client absolutely must converge on the exact same document content, byte for byte, there is no such thing as an acceptable minor discrepancy the way there was with comment ordering in a live chat. At the same time, your own typing has to feel instantaneous, which means the client applies your own keystrokes to its local view before the server has even acknowledged them, and only reconciles afterward if a transform changes anything. Availability here is scoped per document rather than platform-wide, since one document's owning server crashing should never be able to affect a completely unrelated document. And offline tolerance matters because someone genuinely will lose their connection mid-sentence and expect their work to still be there when they reconnect.

blocks.text: This design uses Operational Transformation rather than a CRDT, since OT keeps the per-operation metadata small and matches how the real product was originally built, at the cost of needing a central server per document to establish a global order, a trade-off examined in depth in section 24. Documents are assumed to be plain rich text with basic formatting, complex embedded objects like spreadsheets or drawings are out of scope. A typical document has a small number of concurrent editors, a handful to a few dozen, rather than thousands, though the design calls out explicitly what breaks if that assumption is wrong. Version history is checkpoint-based rather than a fully restorable state after every single keystroke.

blocks.text: Say the platform stores a hundred million documents in total, the overwhelming majority of them sitting untouched at any given moment. Of those, only a few hundred thousand are being actively edited at once across the whole platform. The number that actually matters for this design is not the total document count, it is the concurrency on any one document: a typical actively edited document has a handful of simultaneous editors, rarely more than a few dozen, generating something on the order of ten operations per second between them. That is a tiny number compared to the million-viewer fan-out problem a live chat system faces, and it is exactly why this design can afford a single owning server per document rather than needing to shard a single document's traffic the way a viral livestream needs to shard its viewers.

blocks.text: Every document has exactly one OT server instance that owns it for as long as it is being actively edited, and every operation for that document, from every connected client, is routed to that same instance. This single-owner-per-document model is the load-bearing architectural decision in this whole design, because Operational Transformation only works if there is one place establishing a single, agreed-upon order for every operation on a document. A client opens a document over a WebSocket, the router hashes the document id to find its owning instance, and every operation the client sends from then on goes to that same server. The owning server transforms incoming operations against anything that happened concurrently, assigns each one a new revision number, appends it to a durable operation log, and broadcasts the transformed operation to every other connected client. Cursor and presence updates travel a separate, lighter path, since they can tolerate being lossy in a way document edits never can.

blocks.alt: Clients route through a document router to the single OT server owning their document; that server persists operations and snapshots, broadcasts transformed edits back to every client, and a separate presence service carries best-effort cursor updates

blocks.text: The transform step is the actual heart of the system, and it is worth seeing with real numbers rather than only in the abstract. Say the document is "Hello World" and both Alice and Bob are editing from revision 0. Alice inserts "Beautiful " at position 6, meaning right before "World". Bob, at the exact same moment, inserts "!" at position 11, the very end of the original string. The server receives Alice's operation first, applies it, and the document becomes "Hello Beautiful World", now at revision 1. When Bob's operation arrives, it was generated against revision 0 and cannot simply be applied as-is, position 11 in the original string is now the middle of the word "Beautiful". The server transforms Bob's operation against Alice's: since Alice's insertion happened at position 6, which is at or before Bob's original position of 11, Bob's position shifts right by the length of Alice's insertion, 10 characters, landing at position 21, which is exactly the new end of the string. Applying Bob's transformed operation gives "Hello Beautiful World!", and once that transformed operation is broadcast back to both Alice and Bob, they both converge on that exact same final text.

blocks.text: Because a document's operations must be serialized through one place, routing is sticky by document id rather than balanced round-robin the way a stateless API would be. Every operation for document D, from every client editing it, lands on the exact same OT server instance for the entire duration that document is being actively edited.

blocks.text: Every operation submitted over the WebSocket carries the revision number the client last knew about, which is exactly what lets the OT server decide whether that operation needs to be transformed against anything that committed after it.

blocks.alt: Document, Operation, Snapshot, Permission, and User, with Operation carrying the revision number that anchors the whole transform algorithm

blocks.text: The Operation table is append-only, mirroring the operation log directly, and the Snapshot table exists purely as a performance optimization so a freshly opened document does not need to replay its entire history from the very first keystroke ever typed.

blocks.text: This is an event-sourced model: the operation log is the true, authoritative history of a document, and the current document content is a derived value, reconstructable at any point by replaying operations from the nearest snapshot forward. That is precisely what makes an OT server's failover recoverable in section 20, and it is also what version history in section 8 is built directly on top of, since a "version" is nothing more than a snapshot at a particular revision number.

blocks.alt: Alice submits an operation, the server applies and advances the revision, acknowledges Alice, and broadcasts the same operation to Bob
A reconnecting client tells the server its last known revision, and the server replays every operation committed since then before the client resumes sending new edits

blocks.text: The happy path is exactly the worked example from section 7.1: two concurrent inserts, transformed against each other, converging on one final document. The workflow worth walking through separately is what happens to a client that was offline. Suppose that client's last known revision is 5, but the document is now at revision 40 because other people kept editing while it was disconnected. On reconnect, the client does not resend its own already-applied local state as new operations, it sends only whatever it typed while offline, tagged against revision 5, and the server transforms those against everything from revision 6 through 40 before applying them, exactly the same transform machinery used for two clients editing a fraction of a second apart, just applied across a much larger gap.

blocks.alt: Opening an already-active document attaches directly to its in-memory state; opening a dormant one loads the latest snapshot and replays only the operations since it

blocks.text: The real cache here is not a separate caching layer, it is the OT server's own in-memory representation of whichever documents it currently owns and are being actively edited. A document nobody has touched in an hour is not sitting in memory anywhere, it is reconstructed on demand the moment someone opens it again.

blocks.alt: The OT server writes accepted operations to persistence asynchronously and triggers snapshot generation on its own schedule, neither of which blocks the live broadcast to connected clients

blocks.text: Persisting an operation durably and broadcasting it to other clients are decoupled on purpose: a client should see another editor's change the instant it is transformed, without waiting on a disk write to confirm first, as long as the write-behind queue itself is durable enough that an acknowledged operation is never actually lost.

blocks.alt: A client opening a document is routed by an edge load balancer to a document router, which sends every operation for that document to its one sticky owning instance

blocks.text: This is a deliberately different shape than balancing stateless HTTP traffic. There is no "any healthy instance will do" here, because only one instance is allowed to be authoritative for a given document's operation order at any moment.

blocks.alt: New OT server instances absorb newly opened documents; an existing document's ownership never moves mid-session, since moving it would require pausing edits to transfer state safely

blocks.text: Scaling this system is really about scaling the number of documents that can be actively owned across the fleet at once, not about scaling any single document's throughput, since a single document's edit volume is small by the numbers in section 6. The one case this does not comfortably cover, a single document with an enormous number of simultaneous editors, is called out directly as a bottleneck in section 23.

blocks.alt: An ordinary document is fully owned and served by one instance; even an unusually large, heavily co-edited document still has exactly one owner, since operations cannot be split across two owners without breaking the single serialization guarantee

blocks.text: This is the opposite of how a live chat system handles its hottest stream. A viral livestream can split its viewers across many gateway shards because delivering a comment to a viewer does not require coordinating with every other viewer. An edit to a document cannot be split that way, because every edit has to be ordered against every other edit to the same document, which is precisely why this is called out as a real, structural bottleneck rather than something scaling fixes.

blocks.alt: Document content is strongly consistent, every client must converge to identical bytes; cursor and presence positions are best-effort, since a moment of staleness there causes no real harm

blocks.text: This is the sharpest contrast with the rest of this HLD category. A chat message being slightly out of order is invisible to users. Two collaborators' documents silently diverging is not invisible, it is a broken product, someone's work either duplicating or disappearing. That is exactly why this design accepts a single point of coordination per document as the cost of the one guarantee that cannot be relaxed.

blocks.alt: When a document's owning instance crashes, the router elects a new owner, which reconstructs the document by loading the latest snapshot and replaying the operation log since it, before clients resume editing

blocks.text: This recovery procedure is the direct payoff of treating the operation log as the authoritative source of truth in section 11. Nothing about a document's state lives only in one server's memory in a way that a snapshot and log replay cannot rebuild.

blocks.alt: A user without at least view access is denied outright; a view-only or comment-only user can connect and watch live edits but has any operation they submit rejected; a full editor can both watch and submit

blocks.text: Permission checks happen both when a client first opens a document and on every individual operation it submits afterward, since a user's access level can be downgraded by someone else while they are still connected, and that change needs to take effect immediately rather than only on the next reconnect.

blocks.text: The metric that matters most here is operation transform latency, the time from a client submitting an operation to receiving its acknowledgment, since that number creeping up is the first sign an OT server instance is overloaded with too many actively owned documents. Alongside it: operation log write lag, snapshot generation lag per document, and failover recovery time, since a slow replay directly extends how long a document is unreachable after its owner crashes.

blocks.alt: A single document owner is an unavoidable serialization point for that document; a mega document with hundreds of simultaneous editors can overload one owner; and infrequent snapshots make failover replay slower than it needs to be

blocks.text: The mega-document case is the one true structural limitation of this design, and it is worth naming honestly rather than papering over: if a single document genuinely needs hundreds or thousands of simultaneous editors, plain per-document OT on one owning instance stops being enough, and the system would need to either batch and coalesce operations more aggressively before they reach the owner, or move toward a CRDT-based model that does not require one serialization point at all.

blocks.alt: Operational Transformation needs a central server to establish ordering but keeps per-operation metadata small; a CRDT needs no central server at all but carries heavier per-character metadata

blocks.text: Operational Transformation is the right choice here because it matches the concurrency levels from section 6, a handful of editors per document, where a single owning server is a perfectly reasonable coordination point and the metadata overhead per operation stays small. A CRDT-based design would remove the single-owner bottleneck entirely, letting clients merge edits peer to peer without any central authority, which matters far more for a fully offline-first or massively multi-editor product, at the cost of every character or block needing its own persistent identity and tombstone metadata that never fully goes away, a real storage and complexity cost that is hard to justify at this system's actual scale.

blocks.text: The overwhelming majority of stored documents are not being actively edited at any given moment, from section 6 only a few hundred thousand out of a hundred million are, so keeping an OT server instance's memory footprint tied only to documents someone currently has open, and evicting a document's in-memory state shortly after the last client disconnects, keeps compute cost proportional to actual activity rather than total storage. Snapshot frequency is itself a cost lever: snapshotting too often wastes storage on redundant checkpoints, too rarely makes every reconstruction and failover slower, and the right interval is tuned against how expensive replay actually turns out to be in practice.

items: Two users insert text at the literal same position at the same moment, which the transform algorithm resolves with a consistent tie-breaking rule, such as ordering by client id, so both clients still converge identically.

A client pastes a very large block of text as a single operation, which the transform algorithm has to treat as one atomic insert rather than many tiny ones, to avoid an explosion of per-character operations.
A user issues an undo immediately after someone else's concurrent edit landed, requiring the undo to be transformed against that intervening edit rather than blindly reverting to stale state.

A client reconnects after being offline long enough that the document has been snapshotted several times since, requiring the catch-up flow to still work correctly starting from an old revision number.

blocks.text: Deploying a new version of the OT server needs a drain-and-handoff strategy rather than an abrupt restart, since an instance being redeployed is actively holding live document state for every document it currently owns; ownership needs to transfer cleanly to another instance, with clients briefly reconnecting, rather than the in-flight document state simply being dropped. The transform algorithm itself deserves an especially thorough test suite of concurrent-edit scenarios before any change ships, since a subtle bug there causes silent document divergence rather than a loud, easily caught error.

The transform algorithm itself deserves an especially thorough test suite of concurrent-edit scenarios before any change ships, since a subtle bug there causes silent document divergence rather than a loud, easily caught error.

blocks.text: Migrating toward a CRDT-based model would directly remove the single-owner bottleneck discussed in section 23, at the cost of the metadata overhead discussed in section 24, and would be the natural next step if the product needed to support genuinely massive simultaneous editing on one document. Richer real-time presence, such as showing what paragraph each collaborator is currently reading rather than only where their cursor sits, is a comparatively low-risk addition once the core transform pipeline is solid. Fine-grained, comment-thread-level permissions, separate from document-level view or edit access, would round out the access control model.

items: Architecture: a single-owner-per-document OT server model, with sticky routing, an append-only operation log, periodic snapshots, and a separate best-effort presence path.
Capacity: a hundred million stored documents, a few hundred thousand actively edited at once, typically a handful of concurrent editors and roughly ten operations per second on a busy document.
The core algorithm: Operational Transformation, worked through with real position arithmetic on a concrete two-user concurrent-edit example.
Database: an event-sourced operation log with periodic snapshots, exactly mirroring how version history and crash recovery both work.
End-to-end workflows: edit submission and reconnect-and-catch-up, both traced as sequence diagrams.

Consistency: strong, byte-for-byte convergence for document content, deliberately the opposite trade from the loose consistency used elsewhere in this HLD category, with best-effort presence data kept separate.

Trade-offs: Operational Transformation versus a CRDT-based design, and the honest limitation that a single document with an extreme number of simultaneous editors is a real structural bottleneck this design does not fully solve.
